**The Boeing X-50A Dragonfly existed to demonstrate one manoeuvre. It flew nine times across two airframes and three years, was destroyed twice, and never attempted that manoeuvre once.** Both losses happened at low speed, in the flight regime the aeroplane shared with every helicopter ever built, and neither had anything directly to do with the conversion the programme was funded to prove [[Boeing X-50 Dragonfly][ref_x50_wikipedia]] [[DARPA pulls plug on X-50 stopped-rotor concept, FlightGlobal][ref_flightglobal_cancel]].

This is the fifty-first article in the [X-Planes series][related_post_a297_framing], following the [X-1][related_post_a298_bell_x1], the [X-2][related_post_a299_bell_x2], the **This article argues that the two are not independent.** The design choices that make a rotor safe to stop in flight are the same choices that made this aeroplane difficult to hover, and the connection runs through the size of the surfaces that had to carry the weight while the rotor was unloaded.

## The Designation Is a Claim About the Concept

**The number was chosen rather than assigned in sequence.** The specialist designation directory records that the X-50A received a round number deliberately, on the reasoning that a canard rotor wing is a fifty-fifty mixture of helicopter and aeroplane [[Boeing X-50, Directory of U.S. Military Rockets and Missiles][ref_x50_designation]]. Boeing had named the vehicle Dragonfly in 1998 and the designation followed in 2002.

**This is the second consecutive article in which the numbering carries an argument.** The [X-49][related_post_a346_piasecki_x49] was skipped in 2002 and filled in 2004, and the reason the number was available at all is that it had been reserved for something that had not yet been assigned. The X-50 took the round number because somebody thought the concept deserved it.

**A designation is a claim made before the evidence arrives, and this one was falsified.** A fifty-fifty mixture of two flight regimes is a description of an aspiration. The aeroplane demonstrated the helicopter half badly and the aeroplane half not at all.

## The Research Question

**Can a rotor be stopped in flight and used as a wing, and can it be started again.**

That question is older than the aeroplane by forty years and it has never received a flight-test answer. The X-50A was the second serious attempt to obtain one and the first to leave the ground.

## Programme Origin

**The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency [[Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency][ref_darpa]] and Boeing signed a fifty-fifty cost-sharing agreement in June 1998 worth twenty-four million dollars over thirty-seven months, with a flight demonstration planned for early 2001** [[Dragonfly canard rotor wing unmanned aerial vehicle, Federation of American Scientists][ref_fas_crw]]. The work was carried out by Boeing Phantom Works [[Phantom Works][ref_phantom_works]]. The concept came to Boeing through its acquisition of McDonnell Douglas, which had studied the canard rotor wing through the 1990s and had run a low-speed wind tunnel entry in 1993 [[Bass, Thompson, Rutherford and Swanson, Low-speed wind tunnel test results of the canard rotor/wing concept][research_crw_lowspeed_tunnel]].

**The first hover flight took place in December 2003 and the programme was terminated in September 2006.** Against a thirty-seven month plan that is ninety-nine months, a factor of

$$
\frac{99}{37} = 2.68
$$

**and the demonstration the money was for never happened.** Two airframes were built and both were destroyed, so the twenty-four million dollars bought twelve million dollars per airframe and nine flights.

**The predecessor matters and the article returns to it.** The Sikorsky S-72 Rotor Systems Research Aircraft was modified from 1983 to carry an X-wing circulation control rotor, was rolled out in 1986, never flew in that configuration and was cancelled in 1988 [[Sikorsky S-72][ref_s72_wikipedia]] [[Sikorsky X-Wing, Igor I. Sikorsky Historical Archives][ref_sikorsky_xwing]]. **The X-50A was flying eighteen years after the previous stopped-rotor programme was abandoned**, and it ended the same way, which is to say without a conversion.

## What Happens to a Rotor That Stops

### The Advance Ratio Has No Upper Bound

The advance ratio relates flight speed to rotor tip speed and it is the variable the previous article in this series was about.

$$
\mu = \frac{V}{\Omega R}
$$

**A conventional rotor becomes untrimmable somewhere near** $\mu = 0.40$ [[Compound helicopter][ref_compound_wikipedia]] **and the X-49A reached 0.441, which is close to the best a compound helicopter has demonstrated** [[Piasecki X-49 SpeedHawk][ref_x49_wikipedia]]. The X-49 existed to push that number up by a little.

**The X-50 had to pass through all of it.** As $\Omega \rightarrow 0$ at constant flight speed, the advance ratio grows without bound.

$$
\lim_{\Omega \to 0} \frac{V}{\Omega R} = \infty
$$

**The rotor tip speed of the X-50A is not published in any source consulted**, so the entry condition is computed across the range conventional practice would suggest. At the 130 knot conversion condition the one public computational study uses [[Pandya and Aftosmis, Computation of external aerodynamics for a canard rotor/wing aircraft][research_pandya_aftosmis]], a tip speed of 500 feet per second gives $\mu = 0.439$ and a tip speed of 700 feet per second gives $\mu = 0.313$. The tip speed that would place the entry exactly at the conventional limit is

$$
\Omega R = \frac{V}{0.40} = \frac{219.4}{0.40} = 548.5 \ \mathrm{ft/s}
$$

**which sits in the middle of that range.** So the X-50A most likely began its conversion at about the advance ratio where the X-49A ran out of aeroplane, and then went further in the one direction no conventional rotor can go.

### Lift Falls With the Square of Rotor Speed

Rotor thrust in hover follows from the thrust coefficient, in the standard form used throughout the rotorcraft literature [[Leishman, Principles of helicopter aerodynamics][book_leishman]] [[Johnson, Helicopter theory][book_johnson_helicopter_theory]] [[Seddon, Basic helicopter aerodynamics][book_seddon]].

$$
T = C_T \rho A (\Omega R)^2
$$

**Halving the rotor speed quarters the available thrust at constant thrust coefficient.** A rotor that is slowing to a stop is therefore losing its lift on a square law, and it loses it fastest at the end. There is no rotor speed at which the surface stops being a rotor and starts being a wing. There is a continuous handover, and the handover has to be completed before the rotor speed reaches the value at which the rotor cannot carry the aircraft.

### Unloading Is the Only Way Through

**The X-wing programme established what happens if the handover is not completed.** The 2001 computational study opens by recording that analysis and testing of the X-wing found high transient aerodynamic loads during conversion, and that the canard rotor wing design addresses this by generating positive lift on both the canard and the horizontal tail so that the main rotor can be completely unloaded throughout the conversion manoeuvre [[Pandya and Aftosmis, Computation of external aerodynamics for a canard rotor/wing aircraft][research_pandya_aftosmis]].

**An unloaded rotor does not stall, whatever its advance ratio.** That is the trick, and it is a good one. Retreating blade stall is a consequence of demanding lift from a blade with insufficient dynamic pressure, and a blade asked for no lift cannot be asked for too much. The reverse flow region can cover the entire disc without consequence if the disc is carrying nothing.

**The price is that the weight has to go somewhere, and it goes onto the canard and the horizontal tail.** Everything that follows in this article is a consequence of that sentence.

## The Surfaces That Carry the Weight Instead

### How Large They Have to Be

At the conversion condition the canard and tail carry the entire aircraft. The dynamic pressure at 130 knots at sea level is

$$
q = \tfrac{1}{2} \rho V^2 = \tfrac{1}{2} (0.0023769)(219.4)^2 = 57.2 \ \mathrm{lbf/ft^2}
$$

and the area required to carry the gross weight follows.

$$
S = \frac{W}{q \, C_L}
$$

**At a lift coefficient of 1.2, which a flapped canard and a full-flying tail can reach, the required area is 21.3 square feet. At 0.8 it is 31.9 square feet.** The published gross weight of 1,460 pounds is Boeing's own figure at first flight [[The revolutionary Boeing Canard Rotor/Wing aircraft begins flight testing][ref_boeing_first_flight]].

### Where They Have to Sit

**The rotor is twelve feet in diameter and the disc area is 113.1 square feet.** The required lifting area is therefore between 18.8 and 28.2 percent of the rotor disc, and those surfaces are mounted fore and aft on a fuselage 17.7 feet long, which is 1.475 times the rotor diameter.

**The spans say it more directly.** The canard spans 8.9 feet and the horizontal tail 8.1 feet, against a rotor diameter of twelve feet.

$$
\frac{b_{\text{canard}}}{D} = 0.742 \qquad \frac{b_{\text{tail}}}{D} = 0.675
$$

**Two lifting surfaces, each spanning between two thirds and three quarters of the rotor diameter, sit directly underneath the rotor.** On a conventional helicopter the horizontal stabiliser spans a small fraction of the rotor diameter and exists to trim the aircraft rather than to carry it. Here both surfaces exist to carry the whole aircraft, and that requirement sets their size.

### The Result That Decides the Article

**The rotor is small because it has to be a wing, and the wings are large because they have to be a rotor substitute.** These two facts are the same design decision seen from opposite ends, and together they produce a disc loading no helicopter of this weight would otherwise have.

$$
\frac{W}{A} = \frac{1460}{113.1} = 12.9 \ \mathrm{lbf/ft^2}
$$

**That is 1.34 times the disc loading computed for the X-49A in the previous article**, on an aeroplane one fifteenth of its weight. The hover induced velocity follows from momentum theory [[Gessow and Myers, Aerodynamics of the helicopter][book_gessow]] [[Bramwell, Bramwell's helicopter dynamics][book_bramwell]].

$$
v_i = \sqrt{\frac{W}{2 \rho A}} = \sqrt{\frac{12.9}{2(0.0023769)}} = 52.1 \ \mathrm{ft/s}
$$

The fully developed slipstream moves at twice that, being 104.2 feet per second or 61.75 knots, and its dynamic pressure is equal to the disc loading exactly.

$$
q_{\text{slip}} = \tfrac{1}{2} \rho (2 v_i)^2 = \frac{W}{A} = 12.9 \ \mathrm{lbf/ft^2}
$$

**So between 21 and 32 square feet of lifting surface sits in a 12.9 pound per square foot slipstream in hover.** Taking a drag coefficient of unity for surfaces with flaps deployed gives a download of 12.9 pounds per square foot, and against the mid-range area of 21.3 square feet that is 22.6 percent of the gross weight. At a drag coefficient of 0.6 it is 13.5 percent and at 1.2 it is 27.1 percent.

**The download is not the point, though it is large.** The point is what happens to that force as the aircraft begins to move forward.

**In hover the wake goes straight down and both surfaces are in it.** The canard is ahead of the centre of gravity and the tail behind it, so the two downloads produce opposing pitching moments that partly cancel. **As the aircraft accelerates the wake skews aft.** The canard comes out of the wake first and the tail stays in it longest. The forward download disappears while the aft download remains, and the residual is a nose-up pitching moment that grows with airspeed.

**This is a known effect on conventional helicopters and it is why many of them carry a programmable stabilator** [[Prouty, Helicopter performance, stability and control][book_prouty]] [[Padfield, Helicopter flight dynamics][book_padfield]]. On the X-50A the surface concerned spans two thirds of the rotor diameter and is sized to carry the entire aircraft, so the effect is not a trim nuisance. It is a large moment produced by a large surface, and it appears in exactly the speed range between hover and conversion entry.

## Driving a Rotor From Its Tips

### What Reaction Drive Deletes

**The X-50A had no gearbox, no driveshaft and no tail rotor.** During rotary-wing flight the exhaust of the Williams F112 turbofan was diverted through the rotor hub, out along the blades and through nozzles at the tips [[The revolutionary Boeing Canard Rotor/Wing aircraft begins flight testing][ref_boeing_first_flight]] [[Williams F112][ref_f112_wikipedia]]. As the canard and tail took up the load the exhaust was progressively diverted to a nozzle at the rear.

**A tip-driven rotor applies no torque to the airframe**, because the force turning it acts at the blade tips rather than through a shaft. That deletes the anti-torque requirement entirely, and with it the tail rotor, its driveshaft, its gearbox and the power they consume. On a machine that also has to stop its rotor in flight this is more than a weight saving. **A stopped shaft-driven rotor would still have a transmission attached to it, and the torque path would have to be broken and remade.**

### What It Charges Instead

**The efficiency of a jet doing work on a body moving at speed** $V$ **is the Froude efficiency.**

$$
\eta = \frac{2}{1 + V_j / V}
$$

For a tip jet the relevant body speed is the rotor tip speed. **Neither the tip speed nor the exhaust velocity is published for this aeroplane**, so the result is computed across the plausible ranges. At a tip speed of 700 feet per second and an exhaust velocity of 1,400 feet per second the efficiency is 0.667. At a tip speed of 500 and an exhaust velocity of 2,000 it is 0.400.

**A mechanical rotor transmission runs at about 0.97.** The reaction drive therefore costs a factor of between

$$
\frac{0.97}{0.667} = 1.5 \qquad \text{and} \qquad \frac{0.97}{0.400} = 2.4
$$

**in the power required to turn the rotor.** That is a first-order figure and it ignores the pressure losses of ducting hot gas through a rotating hub and along a rotating blade, which are real and which make the true penalty worse rather than better.

**The idea had already carried passengers.** The Fairey Rotodyne of 1957 drove its rotor with tip jets, demonstrated the configuration at scale and was cancelled on cost and on noise [[Fairey Rotodyne][ref_fairey_rotodyne]].

**This is why reaction drive keeps being reinvented and keeps not winning.** The weight it saves is immediate and visible on a drawing. The fuel it burns is a factor of 1.5 to 2.4, and it appears only in the range column.

**The engine is a cruise missile engine in the 600 to 730 pound thrust class.** Against a gross weight of 1,460 pounds the raw thrust-to-weight ratio is between 0.41 and 0.50, so the aeroplane cannot hover on direct jet thrust. **The rotor is what makes vertical flight possible at all**, converting that thrust into between 2.0 and 2.4 times as much lift, and the article's disc-loading arithmetic is the measure of how hard it has to work to do so.

## The Section That Has to Work in Both Directions

**When the rotor stops, one blade points left and the other points right.** The flow arrives at both from the front. On one of them it arrives over what was the trailing edge.

**A conventional aerofoil has a rounded leading edge and a sharp trailing edge and is useless backwards.** The canard rotor wing therefore used an elliptical section, blunt at both ends, with a thickness ratio varying from 24 percent at the root to 16 percent at the tip. That section is a compromise between what a rotor blade wants and what a stopped wing wants, and it is optimal for neither.

**Twenty-four percent thickness is extraordinary** [[Hoerner, Fluid dynamic drag][book_hoerner_drag]] [[Schlichting and Gersten, Boundary-layer theory][book_schlichting]] [[McCormick, Aerodynamics, aeronautics and flight mechanics][book_mccormick]]. A transport wing runs near 12 percent and a helicopter blade nearer 9 to 12. The section exists because a blade that must work in reverse flow cannot have a sharp edge anywhere, and because the blade has to be deep enough to duct hot exhaust gas to the tip.

**The elliptical section is a better reverse-flow aerofoil than a conventional symmetric one**, which is the reason it was chosen, and it is a worse aerofoil than either in the regimes where those are used. The stopped-rotor literature has been circling this compromise since the 1960s [[Biggers and Watts, Horizontal stoppable rotor conversion][research_horizontal_stoppable]] [[Ballard, McCloud and Forsyth, An investigation of a stoppable helicopter rotor with circulation control][research_stoppable_circulation]] [[Lance, Sung and Stroub, Low-speed wind-tunnel test of an unpowered high-speed stoppable rotor concept in fixed-wing mode][research_stoppable_fixed_wing_mode]].

## The Aircraft

**The X-50A was unmanned, 17.7 feet long, 6.5 feet high and weighed 1,460 pounds.** It carried a two-bladed teetering rotor twelve feet in diameter, an 8.9 foot canard and an 8.1 foot horizontal tail, and was powered by a single Williams F112 turbofan [[The revolutionary Boeing Canard Rotor/Wing aircraft begins flight testing][ref_boeing_first_flight]] [[Dragonfly canard rotor wing unmanned aerial vehicle, Federation of American Scientists][ref_fas_crw]]. Maximum speed was quoted as 380 knots and cruise as 150 knots, with conversion planned near 120 to 130 knots.

**The sources disagree about the weight and the disagreement is small but real.** Boeing states 1,460 pounds. The general encyclopaedia states an empty weight of 1,265 pounds and a gross weight of 1,422 pounds [[Boeing X-50 Dragonfly][ref_x50_wikipedia]]. The spread between the two gross figures is 38 pounds, or 2.7 percent, and it moves the computed disc loading from 12.9 to 12.6 pounds per square foot. **No conclusion in this article turns on the difference**, and the larger figure is used throughout because it is the manufacturer's own.

**Nothing published gives a weight breakdown**, against a design literature in which one is the starting point [[Raymer, Aircraft design, a conceptual approach][book_raymer]] [[Anderson, Aircraft performance and design][book_anderson_performance]]. The encyclopaedia's pair implies an empty weight fraction of 89.0 percent, which for an unmanned demonstrator carrying no payload is plausible and is not independently confirmed.

## The Flight Test Record

**The first airframe hovered for about eighty seconds in December 2003** at the United States Army Proving Ground at Yuma, Arizona [[The revolutionary Boeing Canard Rotor/Wing aircraft begins flight testing][ref_boeing_first_flight]] [[Yuma Proving Ground][ref_yuma]]. **The general encyclopaedia dates the first flight to 24 November 2003 and the designation directory to 4 December 2003**, while the manufacturer's own announcement is dated 4 December and describes a flight that had already occurred. The article does not resolve this and records it as unresolved.

**On its third flight, on 23 March 2004, the first airframe was destroyed.** The cause was recorded as cross coupling of the rotor controls.

**The second airframe resumed flight testing in November and December 2005** [[Second Boeing X-50A Dragonfly Canard Rotor/Wing prototype completes hover flight][ref_boeing_second_hover]]. **On 12 April 2006, on the sixth of eleven planned flights, it was destroyed at the same range.** The investigation concluded that the aircraft was lost to insufficient low-speed control authority, which is a statement about control power against a moment in the sense the flight dynamics literature uses [[Etkin and Reid, Dynamics of flight][book_etkin]], and that the fuselage was subject to an aerodynamic pitching moment of extreme sensitivity, with both airspeed and rotor wake producing a nose-up pitching motion greater than the flight controls could compensate for.

**DARPA withdrew funding in September 2006** [[DARPA pulls plug on X-50 stopped-rotor concept, FlightGlobal][ref_flightglobal_cancel]].

**Nine flights across two airframes. No conversion was attempted on any of them.**

## What the Analysis Said and What the Aircraft Did

### The Computation Named the Mechanism

**In 2001, five years before the second loss, two researchers at the NASA Ames Research Center published an inviscid computational study of this exact aeroplane at its conversion condition** [[Pandya and Aftosmis, Computation of external aerodynamics for a canard rotor/wing aircraft][research_pandya_aftosmis]]. They solved the Euler equations on Cartesian meshes of roughly nine million cells, at seven rotor azimuth positions covering a quarter turn, at Mach 0.1986 and zero angle of attack.

**They found that the rotor was indeed unloaded and that the canard and horizontal tail could carry the weight of the aircraft**, which was the question they were asked. They also found something they were not looking for.

**They identified upwash from the forward fuselage as a source of positive pitching moment on the rotor**, and they wrote that no change to the geometry of the hub area can relieve the upwash from the forward fuselage, and that the effect of the upwash is therefore the limiting case for the load variations experienced by this vehicle.

**A nose-up pitching moment produced by the forward fuselage, which no local geometry change can remove.** Five years later the second airframe was lost to a nose-up pitching moment of extreme sensitivity attributed to the fuselage.

### It Also Cleared the Margin

**The same paper concludes that the amplitudes of the moments are well within the authority of the control surfaces.**

**The mechanism was identified correctly and the margin was assessed as adequate.** One of those two judgements survived contact with the aeroplane.

### These Are Not the Same Flight Condition

**The honest statement of the relationship is narrower than the coincidence suggests, and the article states it narrowly.**

**The 2001 computation was performed at 130 knots, in conversion.** The 2006 accident occurred at low speed, in the regime between hover and conversion entry. These are different flight conditions, and a result computed at one does not transfer to the other. The paper was not wrong about the case it examined. **It was never asked about the case that mattered.**

**That is the finding, and it is a finding about where analysis effort goes rather than about a mistaken calculation.** The X-wing's recorded lesson was that the severe loads arrive during conversion, and specifically during the last few revolutions when the rotor turns slowly [[Corliss, Dunn and Morrison, RSRA/X-Wing flight control system development, lessons learned][research_rsra_xwing_lessons]]. The community believed conversion was the hard part, because the previous programme had said so. **So conversion was computed, and wind-tunnel tested, and cleared. The low-speed regime was the part everybody already knew how to do.**

**There is a further limitation and it is in the method rather than the framing.** The Euler equations carry no viscosity. A hemispherical hub beneath a stopped rotor above a bluff fuselage is a separation problem, and an inviscid solver cannot represent separation. The paper is explicit that it is inviscid and does not overclaim, and the limitation is recorded here because the sensitivity that killed the aeroplane is of exactly the kind an inviscid method cannot see.

**The paper also states that its force and moment values could not be published, being proprietary, so its figures carry no numbers on the vertical axis.** The only public computational assessment of this aeroplane's conversion loads is therefore unavailable in magnitude to anybody outside the programme.

## Where the Framing Breaks Down

**The chain of reasoning in this article is a chain of plausible inferences and not a demonstrated causal account, and four links are weaker than the others.**

**First, the article claims the wake-skew pitch-up mechanism without direct evidence that it was the mechanism.** The accident finding is a nose-up pitching moment from airspeed and rotor wake exceeding control authority. That the specific route was the tail remaining in the wake as the canard left it is the standard explanation for that signature on rotorcraft, and it is consistent with the geometry, and it is not stated in any source consulted about this aeroplane. **It is an inference from configuration and it is offered as one.**

**Second, the surface areas are derived and not published.** The canard and tail areas are computed from the requirement to carry the aircraft at the published conversion speed, under an assumed lift coefficient range. If the real surfaces are substantially larger, because they were sized by a stall margin rather than by cruise lift, then the download and moment arguments strengthen. If they are smaller, the arguments weaken. **The spans are published and the areas are not, and the spans alone carry the geometric part of the argument.**

**Third, the tip speed is unknown and three results depend on it.** The advance ratio at conversion entry, the hover tip Mach number and the reaction drive efficiency all move with it. The article reports ranges rather than values for all three, and the range for the Froude efficiency is wide enough that the conclusion is qualitative rather than quantitative.

**Fourth, the connection between the 2001 paper and the 2006 accident is a connection of mechanism and not of flight condition.** This is stated at length in the preceding section because it is the single place where this article would most easily overclaim.

**A fifth item is smaller and should be recorded anyway.** The one Mach number published for this aeroplane's conversion condition, being 0.1986 at 130 knots, corresponds to a speed of sound of about 1,105 feet per second rather than the sea level value of 1,116.4 [[U.S. Standard Atmosphere][ref_us_standard_atmosphere_ref]] [[U.S. Standard Atmosphere, 1976][research_us_standard_atmosphere]]. Recomputing 130 knots against the sea level speed of sound gives Mach 0.1965. **The two figures in the source are mutually consistent only at an altitude of roughly two thousand feet**, which is unremarkable for Yuma and is noted so that a reader recomputing the number is not confused by the discrepancy.

### Handling qualities and rotorcraft flight test

**How a rotorcraft is judged rather than merely measured.** Handling qualities criteria, pilot rating scales, flight test technique, simulation and envelope expansion. **Six flights and three flights are the whole flight record of this programme**, so the methodology literature is larger than the data it would have been applied to.

### Rotor wake, airframe interaction and download

**What a rotor does to whatever sits underneath it.** Interactional aerodynamics, wake impingement on tail surfaces, download and inflow. **This aeroplane put two large lifting surfaces directly beneath a small rotor**, and this cluster holds the literature for what that costs in hover and in the transition out of it.

### Elliptical and thick aerofoils, and flow that reverses

**The section a stopped rotor is forced to use.** Elliptical, blunt and symmetric profiles, reverse flow, leading-edge separation bubbles and thick sections. **The X-50A's section was elliptical at 24 percent thickness at the root**, because a blade that becomes a wing must work with the flow arriving from either end.

### Rotor aeromechanics, blade loads and airloads

**How a rotor is actually computed.** Blade element and momentum theory, inflow models, free wake methods, flapping and comprehensive analysis. **The relation that governs this article is elementary in this discipline**, being that lift falls with the square of rotor speed, and its consequences are not.

**The geometry a rotor turns into when it stops.** Low aspect ratio, slender and delta planforms, finite span effects and lifting-line theory. **A twelve-foot rotor is a twelve-foot wing**, and a wing of that span on an aeroplane of this weight is a stub rather than a wing.

### Reaction drive, tip jets and blown rotors

**The second declared family, and the oldest idea in the aeroplane.** Tip jets, pressure jets, reaction drive, circulation control and blown surfaces. **Driving a rotor from its tips deletes the gearbox, the driveshaft and the tail rotor at once**, and this cluster holds the literature for what it charges in their place.

### Canard and close-coupled lifting surfaces

**The surfaces that had to carry the aircraft while the rotor stopped.** Canard and wing interference, upwash, downwash, close-coupled and tandem arrangements, and forebody effects. **A canard is unusual on a rotorcraft and mandatory on this one**, because the weight has to go somewhere during conversion.

The X-50 tried to pass through every value of it**, which is a different problem with the same variable.

### Vibration, fatigue and the loads a rotor imposes

**The loads a rotor sends into the airframe, and what happens as it slows.** Oscillatory hub loads, fatigue, aeroelasticity, flutter and transient loading. **The X-wing's recorded lesson was that the worst loads arrive during the last few revolutions**, when the rotor turns slowly and the flow has time to respond.

### Stopped rotors, the X-wing and the conversion problem

**The keystone, and the smallest substantive cluster in the survey.** Stopped and stoppable rotors, the X-wing, convertible aircraft, conversion corridors and rotor unloading. **It is small because the idea has been tried roughly once a decade since the 1960s and abandoned every time**, so the literature is a series of separate beginnings rather than an accumulation. A probe measured this subject at 30 records in this article's own phrasing and 167 in the field's, and the broader figure is the honest one.

## The Source Base

**The survey rests on 6,042 research records assembled from Crossref, the NASA Technical Reports Server and the Defense Technical Information Center**, of which 824 are report primaries, being 13.6 percent. **Primacy is derived from the identifier rather than from which sweep returned the record**, being a NASA Technical Reports Server address or the Defense Technical Information Center digital object identifier prefix, after A345 found 133 of its own report primaries counted as secondary because the label was inherited from the harvest.

### The Results Probe Was Run Before the Article Was Written

**A340 through A346 all found, at their publication review, that the survey under-covered the article's own conclusions.** That is the fourth pass and the most expensive place to discover it. **A345 and A346 then found that most subjects measured thin only because they were being asked for in the article's phrasing rather than the field's.**

**Both measurements were made here at the draft pass, before the prose existed.** Eight subjects were probed and the result is tabulated below.

| Subject | Article's words | Field's words |
|---|---|---|
| the stopped rotor and its conversion | 30 | 167 |
| the conversion corridor | 5 | 95 |
| reaction drive | 28 | 258 |
| control authority | 14 | 24 |
| the elliptical section | 7 | 236 |
| rotor wake on the tail | 0 | 140 |
| pitch-up at low speed | 3 | 111 |
| the low aspect ratio wing | 140 | 219 |

**Seven of the eight opened by a factor between two and infinity on rephrasing alone.** The eighth moved from 14 to 24.

**That eighth is the subject both airframes were lost to**, so a supplementary harvest was run for it at the draft pass rather than deferred. Fourteen Crossref queries, six against the NASA Technical Reports Server and three against the Defense Technical Information Center were added, asking for control power in hover, control margin, actuator saturation, loss of control and low-speed pitch-up directly. **The subject now stands at 160 records in the field's words and the cluster holds 941.**

### The Gate Was Audited Four Times and Changed Every Time

**The two-sided random audit found defects in both directions on every reading.** The kept side gave up palladium-catalysed cross-coupling chemistry, Darrieus and Savonius wind turbines, an electrical machine rotor, petroleum gas lift, turbine blade internal cooling, turbomachinery compressor aerodynamics and atmospheric chemistry. The dropped side gave up lifting-line theory, static stability, tangential jet blowing, an unstructured Euler solver, bare aircraft flight control and forebody vortex control.

**Eleven homonym families were predicted in advance and four of them actually occurred.** The NASA Dragonfly mission to Titan, elliptic curves and elliptical galaxies, the canard as a duck, the hub as a gene, the wake as the opposite of sleep, energy and chemical conversion, and the general medical bleed were all anticipated and all measured at zero in this pool. **That ratio is the reason the shared sweep store admits only observed patterns**, and the eight families that did occur have been recorded there with the incident that produced each.

### The Residual Was a Fact About the Clusterer

**The unclustered residual stood at 1,355 records, being a quarter of the pool.** Reading a sample of thirty-four showed it was almost entirely on-subject rotorcraft flight-control, wake and flight-test literature that the cluster patterns refused on adjacency while the gate had admitted it on a broader anchor. **Widening the cluster patterns to match the gate moved 479 records into substantive clusters** and the control cluster grew from 96 to 522 before the supplementary harvest raised it further.

### Nine of Ten Book Identifiers Pointed at Unrelated Works

**The hand-written book list inherited from A346 was checked against the repository for the first time and nine of its ten identifiers were wrong.** `Leishman, Principles of helicopter aerodynamics` resolved to a market outlook for dark rum in Japan. `Prouty, Helicopter performance, stability and control` resolved to a book about buying apartment buildings. `Stepniewski and Keys, Rotary-wing aerodynamics` resolved to a work on rural modernisation.

**Every existing check passed on all nine.** The link resolved, so a status check was satisfied. The reference block was well formed, so the corpus verifier was satisfied. The rendered page displayed the label the article had written, so the rendered audit saw nothing. **A citation whose text is correct and whose target is wrong is invisible to every check that does not read the target, and this corpus had none.**

**The measured scope was 510 distinct work keys across 40 files.** Of the 215 keys carrying a title-style label, 19 disagreed with the repository, and every one of those was in an unpublished draft. **That is luck and not process.** `_lib/booklinks.py` now performs the comparison and is covered by three tests, and the two books for which no repository record could be found have been dropped from this article rather than guessed at.

### One Identifier in This Article Was Fabricated and Caught Before Assembly

**A NASA Technical Reports Server identifier for the 1992 report `Smoother conversion from helicopter to airplane` was written from the title rather than looked up, and it did not resolve.** It was found because every foundational identifier in this article was verified against the repository before assembly rather than after. The correct record was located and substituted. **A fabricated citation that renders correctly is the same defect class as the book identifiers above and it was found by the same habit.**

### Four Numbers Sit Exactly on a Rounding Boundary

**The number verifier disagreed with the article four times and every disagreement was a tie.** The reaction drive penalties compute to exactly 1.455 and 2.425, the fuselage length over rotor diameter to exactly 1.475, and the slipstream velocity to exactly 61.75 knots. **At the precision first written, each of those is a coin toss between two representations**, and the article and the checker had called it differently.

**The rule adopted is to state such a value at a precision where it is not a tie**, which meant one fewer decimal for the two penalties and one more for the other two. **The alternative of picking a rounding convention and asserting it would have made the disagreement invisible rather than absent.**

### The Designation Directory Has an Entry This Time

**A346 was the first article in fifty with no page in the specialist designation directory.** The X-50 has one, and it is the source for the claim that the number was chosen for its roundness. The gap at the X-49 was a fact about that aeroplane rather than a change in the source.

## Epistemic State

### Historical Fact

The programme dates, the cost-sharing arrangement, the dimensions, the engine, the two crash dates, the recorded causes and the termination are drawn from the manufacturer's announcements, the specialist designation directory, the Federation of American Scientists and the general press, and are consistent across them except where noted.

### Verified by Independent Derivation

The disc area, disc loading, induced velocity, slipstream dynamic pressure, dynamic pressure at conversion, required lifting area, span fractions, advance ratios, Froude efficiencies, thrust-to-weight ratios and the schedule ratio are computed in this article from published inputs and are reproducible from them.

### Analysis

The identification of surface sizing as the link between conversion safety and hover difficulty, the reading of the reaction drive trade, and the assessment of the elliptical section as a compromise optimal for neither regime.

### Inference

The wake-skew mechanism for the nose-up pitching moment, the relationship between the 2001 computational finding and the 2006 accident, and the claim that analysis effort was directed at conversion because the X-wing had taught that conversion was the hard part.

### What the Record Does Not Settle

Whether the conversion would have worked. **The manoeuvre was never attempted in flight, by this aeroplane or by any other.** Nothing in the flight record bears on the question the programme was funded to answer, and this article makes no claim about it in either direction.

## Out of Scope

Rotor system structural design, the detailed control law implementation, the ducted propulsor family covered in the previous article, and the wider unmanned combat aircraft programmes of the same period.

## Conclusion

**The X-50A Dragonfly took a round designation on the claim that it was half helicopter and half aeroplane. It never demonstrated the aeroplane half, and it was destroyed twice doing the helicopter half.**

**The two facts are connected, and the connection is the size of the tail surfaces.** Stopping a rotor in flight is survivable only if the rotor is unloaded first, and unloading it means something else must carry the aircraft at conversion speed. On a machine this small that means a canard and a tail spanning three quarters and two thirds of the rotor diameter, sitting under a rotor whose disc loading is a third higher than a Black Hawk's because the same surface has to serve as a wing at 380 knots. **The configuration that makes conversion safe puts two large lifting surfaces in a fast slipstream, and then asks the flight control system to hold the aircraft steady while the wake skews off one of them and stays on the other.**

**Both airframes were lost in that speed range.** The 2001 computational study had already named the forebody upwash as a source of nose-up pitching moment and had already said that no local geometry change could remove it. **What it had not been asked was whether the same mechanism had enough authority against it at low speed, because the X-wing had taught everybody that conversion was where the danger lived.**

**Eighteen years separated the cancellation of the X-wing from the loss of the second Dragonfly, and the two programmes have the same result to report.** No rotor has ever been stopped and restarted in flight on an aircraft in a flight test programme. The idea remains exactly as plausible and exactly as unproven as it was in 1988.
